n: David flees Naioth and comes to Jonathan in anguish: what have I done wrong that your father wants to kill me?
Jonathan can't believe it. He insists his father tells him everything and wouldn't hide such a plan from him. Perhaps he trusts Saul's oath from 19:6.

f.g: Far from it! May it never be!

n: David swears that Saul knows of their friendship and is hiding his plans from Jonathan. David feels there is only one step between him and death.

f.w: there is but a step between me and death
f.g: a vivid image of how close the danger is

n: Jonathan offers to do whatever David asks — the response of a true friend.
David proposes a test. Tomorrow is the new moon feast, when he is expected at the king's table. He will hide in the field instead for three days.

f.g: A monthly religious festival with sacrifices and a meal.

n: If Saul asks about him, Jonathan should say David asked permission to go to a family sacrifice in Bethlehem.

f.g: asked permission

n: If Saul says, “Fine,” David is safe. But if Saul is furious, it means he is determined to harm David.

f.g: he has decided to do harm

n: David appeals to their covenant made before the Lord. If he is guilty, he asks Jonathan to kill him himself rather than hand him to Saul.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — show covenant loyalty.

n: Jonathan protests: of course he would tell David if he knew his father planned to harm him.

f.g: Never! Don't even think it!

n: David asks practically: how will he find out, especially if Saul responds harshly?
Jonathan leads David out to the field, away from listening ears.
Jonathan makes a solemn vow before the Lord: after he sounds out his father, if things are good for David, he will send word.

f.g: tested, probed to find out

n: Under a strong oath, Jonathan promises to warn David if Saul means harm and to send him off in peace. He prays the Lord will be with David as He once was with Saul — he seems to sense David will be king.

f.w: The LORD do so and much more to Jonathan
f.g: a self-curse oath — may God punish me if I fail

n: Jonathan asks David, in return, to show him the Lord's kind of loyal love as long as he lives, so he will not be killed.

f.g: Loyal love like God's own (ḥesed).

n: He also asks David never to stop showing kindness to his family, even after the Lord destroys all David's enemies. New kings often wiped out the previous royal family.

f.w: thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house

n: Jonathan makes a covenant with David's house, asking the Lord to hold David's enemies accountable.

f.g: demand an accounting, call to justice

n: Jonathan has David renew his oath because he loves him as himself — a friendship rooted in covenant.

f.w: he loved him as he loved his own soul

n: Jonathan points out that David's empty seat will be noticed at the new moon feast.
After three days, David is to go to his earlier hiding place and wait by the stone Ezel.

f.g: Possibly “stone of departure”; the meaning is uncertain.

f.w: when the business was in hand
f.g: probably referring to the earlier incident in 19:2-3

n: Jonathan will shoot three arrows near the stone, as though practicing at a target.
He will send a boy to retrieve them. If he says the arrows are on this side, David may come — he is safe.
But if he says the arrows are beyond the boy, David must leave, for the Lord is sending him away.
Jonathan seals their agreement: the Lord is witness between them forever.

f.w: the LORD be between thee and me for ever

n: David hides in the field, and the king sits down to the new moon feast.
Saul sits in his usual seat by the wall. Jonathan sits across, Abner beside Saul, and David's place is empty.

f.g: The Greek version reads “Jonathan sat opposite.”

n: On the first day Saul says nothing, assuming David must be ritually unclean and unable to attend the sacred meal.

f.g: Ritual impurity, such as touching a dead body, would keep someone from a sacred meal.

n: On the second day David's seat is still empty, and Saul asks Jonathan why “the son of Jesse” hasn't come. Refusing to say David's name shows contempt.

f.g: A dismissive way of referring to David.

n: Jonathan gives the agreed answer: David asked to go to Bethlehem.
Jonathan explains that David's brother had required him to attend a family sacrifice.
Saul explodes at Jonathan with a vulgar insult aimed at his mother, accusing him of siding with David to his own shame.

f.w: Thou son of the perverse rebellious woman
f.g: A crude insult, roughly “you son of a rebel.”
shame, disgrace

n: Saul tells Jonathan plainly: as long as David lives, Jonathan will never be king. He orders David brought to be killed. Saul is fighting what God has already decided.

f.w: thou shalt not be established, nor thy kingdom

n: Jonathan courageously asks why David should die — what has he done?
Saul throws a spear at his own son. Now Jonathan knows his father is determined to kill David.

f.w: Saul cast a javelin at him

n: Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger and refuses to eat, grieved for David and for the shame his father brought on him.
In the morning Jonathan goes to the field as agreed, with a young boy.
He tells the boy to run and find the arrows, and shoots an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reaches it, Jonathan calls out, “Isn't the arrow beyond you?” — the signal of danger.
Jonathan shouts, “Hurry! Don't stop!” — words for the boy, but really a message to David. The boy gathers the arrows.

f.g: don't linger

n: The boy understands nothing; only Jonathan and David know the meaning.
Jonathan gives his weapons to the boy and sends him back to town.

f.g: weapons — here, his bow and arrows

n: Once the boy is gone, David comes out, bows three times, and the two friends kiss and weep together, David weeping most of all. A heartbreaking farewell.

f.g: until David wept the most, or recovered himself

n: Jonathan sends David off in peace, recalling their sworn covenant that binds them and their descendants forever. Then they part, each to his own path.

f.w: between my seed and thy seed for ever
